how_it_works: The journal shows these posts, newest first. New posts from https://jamiecatt.substack.com are added automatically by scripts/sync-substack.py (run every 30 minutes by the GitHub Action in .github/workflows/sync-substack.yml).
Photos and videos live in media/posts/ and appear in the html as {{m:filename}}. They are always the full-size originals.
A post shows its own drawing in the journal when index.html has a matching art-post-<key> drawing; otherwise it gets the default notebook drawing.

posts.title: trick or treat
posts.blurb: Halloween is over, but the weekend still haunts me.
posts.html:
Halloween is over, but the weekend still haunts me. And Teo. In a good way.

Every year, we try to spice up the spooky season and see where it takes us. Last year, it was in New Mexico where we witnessed Día de los Muertos. This year, it was in our hometown in Salida where we witnessed a zombie street dance and a variety of over-the-top Dolly Parton costumes.

And since it was our first Halloween with Teo, naturally, I had to get him a costume too.

The trick-or-treating festivities began on October 30th, when we drove to the nearby town of Buena Vista. We were there mainly because I had a Yoga Sculpt class at noon. But since we were already there, why not see what the kiddos were up to with their cute costumes? Teo could join in for fun too.

Before heading on our pre-Halloween walk, we had a light brunch at Veya Coffee Bar. Our recent go-to in town. I’m currently addicted to their Rosemary Ricotta Toast. And of course, their coffee.

After brunch and finishing up some light design work, we started our walk. Teo was a little spooked by the crowd and the little kids squealing and running around in costumes. Eventually, we took him to a quieter trail that led to the other side of town. We walked around four miles, but it didn’t feel like it at all.

The next day, R & I slept in. I got out of bed around noon. A typical weekend ritual for me. We did some chores at home before heading into town. They seem to be never-ending. The chores, I mean. There’s always something that needs fixing, cleaning, or reorganizing.

We left the house around two-thirty in the afternoon, and I thought we were already late to the party. Turns out it was just getting started.

Teo donned his bat costume for the second time. He didn’t mind it one bit. We walked to the park, but the food trucks were still setting up. We made a beeline for them anyway. Open or not, we needed to scout out the food scene pronto.

If there’s one thing I love to see, it’s themed food. Spooky-themed food at that. It just completes the vibe. Witch’s Brew Green Chile Pork Stew. Vampire’s Red Beef Posole. Poison Apple Turnover. Yum, yum, yum.

While we were waiting for our food, I stood amongst the trees and just basked in autumn itself. The yellowing leaves crunching beneath our feet, the soft afternoon light, and the slightly cool weather made the entire park feel cozy.

After a light lunch, we decided to go on a walk. There weren’t many trick-or-treaters out yet since things were just getting started. We got coffee from our go-to, Howl Mercantile & Coffee, then walked our usual path towards Sands Lake. This time, Teo was in my pocket. He was a sleepy bat. Probably still recuperating from the four-mile walk the day before.

After our walk, we headed back to the park. It was almost six in the evening, and the party was now in full swing. Music was blasting. There was a zombie street dance on one side. On the other, a pumpkin drop. I was pleasantly surprised (and impressed) by the costumes all around—from kids to adults to dogs.

Every person we passed by was dressed to kill. I was not. I’d planned on matching Teo’s costume this year, but alas, I got too lazy to draw a bat on my face. Next year, I promised myself.

I haven’t celebrated Halloween like this since I was young. I used to dress up as a little fairy and go trick-or-treating with family friends in their rich neighborhood. Then we’d go back to our friends’ home and check out all the candies we got. Those childhood memories have always felt dear to me. Perhaps due to nostalgia. A season that has passed.

We stayed until the sun had set. Drank warm apple cider and witnessed another zombie street dance.

And somehow, this Halloween reminded me how these moments can bring comfort and joy. Going on cozy autumn walks on our usual trails, ordering our faves from our go-to cafes, eating spooky-themed dishes, and seeing the craft and effort put into costumes.

This Halloween brought me equal parts whimsy, joy, and cozy.

posts.title: … and then there were three
posts.blurb: I had plenty of reasons not to get a dog.
posts.html:
I had plenty of reasons not to get a dog. I loved them, but preferably without their fur all over me.

It hadn’t always been that way. I grew up with dogs. A range of them, actually: Labrador, Shih Tzu, Chihuahua, Poodle. I’m sure I didn’t list them all. But you get the gist.

Somewhere along the way, though, I drifted away from the idea of having pets.

Perhaps it started with my mom constantly reminding me to keep my distance. I was allergic, so she didn’t allow any of our dogs inside our home. Then there was the time I got bitten by five or six Shih Tzus on a neighborhood run. I had to get a rabies shot for that. And the cherry on top? My OCD.

Despite all that, R & I decided to bring home a puppy.

And now, I can finally add Maltipoo to the list above.

When I found Teo’s listing, we were still staying with family in California. The next day, I scheduled a video call with the breeder to meet him. I wanted to see beyond the photos, to sense if he was a match for us.

The moment I saw him on FaceTime, his derpy smile won me over right away. But aside from that, there was a familiar gut feeling. The same one I had when I saw R for the first time.

I just knew. And there was no convincing me otherwise.

I remember lying in bed on that Sunday morning, thinking to myself: Am I really considering adopting a puppy?

It didn’t take me long to make up my mind. Over the past year, I’d occasionally get these sudden puppy crazes. I’d search and browse, but never take it further. This time was different.

When I cautiously brought it up to R later that evening, he strongly disagreed. Partly because of the timing, partly because of the responsibilities of caring for a puppy. But he also knew. This time was different.

He asked if we could wait until we were back home in Colorado and done with all our travels for the year. So I compromised. Sort of.

We’d wait until we were back in Colorado. Just not until all our travels were over. I wasn’t going to wait until next year.

Once we’d committed to bringing him home, my days (and now, my algo) suddenly got filled with all things puppy. But somewhere in the middle of all that, I found unsettling reviews of the breeder. Suddenly, my happy puppy research turned into a spiral. What if he arrives sick? Did I make a mistake with this breeder? Will I regret this?

By then, I’d already made the down payment and we were working with the breeder to arrange Teo’s travel from North Carolina to Denver, where we’d pick him up.

I’d already made my decision, and I was going to see it through. But I wasn’t just going to sit around drowning in my own anxious thoughts. I had to do something about it.

As a type-A person and a designer at an agency where humans and robots work side by side, I turned to the solution I knew best: making my own puppy consultant. Somewhere to turn for information and just a little bit of reassurance.

Yes, you are overthinking. Your research made you anxious, but you can turn it into a checklist of what to screen for once you get Teo, not a prophecy of what will happen. That’s a rational way to think of it.

Just what I needed to hear. Thanks, Perplexity.

So for the next week and a half, I teetered between the excitement of getting ready to bring him home and the worry of what condition he’d arrive in.

When the day finally came, R & I made the three-hour drive from our tiny home in Salida to the big city of Denver, where we were staying for the night. From the passenger seat, I kept checking and rechecking the pickup instructions. They said to head to the cargo area.

Cargo? Why the hell were we driving to cargo? Wasn’t he supposed to arrive with a trusted person?

That was how I found out Teo was flying cargo from Chicago to Denver.

Wait… Chicago? Wasn’t he coming from North Carolina? What the hell was happening?

There had been no heads-up from the breeder. All this time, I’d understood he would be flying in-cabin with a trusted person. Had I known otherwise, I would have been strongly against having a three-month-old puppy travel in cargo.

Between the reviews I’d read and this unexpected change, my mind was already running through everything that could go wrong.

What if he arrives sick, anxious, stressed? What if he’s scared of his crate after this? What if he gets sick on the drive home? What if he struggles to settle in with us?

I guess R was right about waiting. Had I listened to him, I might have spared myself some of this emotional roller coaster. Maybe found a more reputable breeder.

But we were already here. Now where's my puppy?

According to the pickup details, his flight landed at 11:45 AM. We arrived and checked in at noon. It was almost 1:00 PM and they sent a message that he was still in the waiting area. I was getting a little impatient. But at least we had some sort of communication.

Finally, after what felt like hours, we got the message we’d been waiting for. He was at the office, ready to be picked up.

Despite my frustration with the whole cargo ordeal, the moment I saw Teo in his crate I almost cried out of relief.

He seemed curious and engaged. Definitely tired and shaken from the travel. Crate condition? A little messy and smelly. But I already expected that. He wasn't the cleanest pup on arrival, but I was just relieved to finally have him safe in my arms.

After signing the release papers, we headed back to the car to take him out of his crate, clean him up and offer him some water and treats. He immediately took to us and cozied up in my arms during the drive back to the city.

Surprisingly, he did not make a fuss (or throw up) during the hour-long drive. He looked so comfortable and did well considering his long day of travel.

Back in the city, we let Teo stretch his legs and run around while we ran errands. That’s when his playful, goofy personality started coming through. Seeing that reassured me. In the back of my mind, however, the worry was still there. I knew it wouldn’t go away until his first vet checkup.

For now, though, all seemed well.

Sadly, our first day together was a short one. Early the next morning, R & I were flying to Eau Claire, Wisconsin, for our anniversary weekend. We savored those few hours with Teo before dropping him off with his pet sitter.

We said goodbye for now. I knew he was in good hands for the weekend. And our story together is just beginning.

Bringing Teo home made me think about how life rarely unfolds the way you imagine it. One moment, you can’t picture it. The next, it’s happening. You’re living it. Learning to adjust, to make room, and to embrace the change.

Thanks for being here and reading the start of Teo’s story.

Until the next Teo chronicle.

posts.title: returning home
posts.blurb: There’s a peculiar kind of forgetting that isn’t forgetting at all.
posts.html:
There’s a peculiar kind of forgetting that isn’t forgetting at all. When you spend enough time away from something you used to do, your body remembers the motion, but not the ease of it. Like learning figure skating as a child and returning to the ice as an adult1. Wobbly knees, ungraceful strokes and unsure footing. That’s how writing feels now.

I look back at my old pieces and think how diligent and eloquent I used to be. I filled every empty space with reading and writing. I marinated on thoughts, like marinating dinner. Slowly. Obsessively. I became a collector of words and dialogue, the way some people collect souvenirs. I made a habit of pocketing every spark2 I found. It was all instinct, no hesitation.

I kept a running archive of personal musings, excerpts, and bits of dialogue. My journal entries were a perfect streak.

That was all a decade ago.

Writing used to come naturally to me. Things flowed from start to end. But now? I keep pausing mid-thought. What am I really trying to say here? I arrange and rearrange my sentences like puzzle pieces that refuse to fit. Should this be my opening or closing line? Now, I’m distracted. Where was I? I edit first, and keep editing and editing, and write last. What’s the synonym of obsessive?

Writing feels like going back on ice after years off it. Broken rhythm, awkward phrasing and disjointed thoughts.

I’ve been looking back through my archives for permission to write again. But it all feels futile. I don’t feel any connection to my old pieces. They feel too cheesy. Too much.

Of course, I’m not going to write like I used to. I’ve changed. My writing will be a reflection of that too. Whatever shape that takes, I’m here to explore it. This platform will become my new thought archive, a space where I learn how I write now.

I will simply write whatever comes to me. No strings attached.

It’s been a decade since I started to write and publish my musings online. I did it consistently for four years. After a six-year break, I’m ready to come home.

1

An exhilarating, yet not-so-fun, experience. I miss the ice, but I don’t think I’ll ever return to it. Sharp toe picks scare me now.

2

A spark can be anything. A quote here. An overheard conversation there. A poetic sentence. A passing thought. Anything that lingers.
